strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored limitation of video anomaly detection: anomaly labels can change with user intent, policy, or deployment context, and language-conditioned definitions are a natural interface for this problem.

The proposed PreVAD dataset is a potentially valuable contribution, with substantially larger scale, broader anomaly taxonomy, and anomaly descriptions that could benefit future vision-language VAD research.
The empirical section is broad by VAD standards, reporting zero-shot detection across seven datasets and classification on UCF-Crime and XD-Violence, with generally strong results.

The paper includes useful ablations separating the effects of PreVAD, language guidance, dynamic video synthesis, and negative mining, and compares against relevant CLIP/VAD baselines including VadCLIP and PEL.
The method is conceptually simple and builds on established components, which makes the approach relatively easy to understand and likely implementable if code and dataset are released.
weaknesses: The central open-world/concept-drift claim is not convincingly evaluated. Most quantitative experiments use standard dataset labels and class-name prompts, which mainly test cross-dataset zero-shot generalization rather than user-controllable redefinition of anomalies. The actual label-change setting is supported mostly by two qualitative examples.

The formal claim that conditioning on a textual anomaly definition avoids concept drift is too strong. In practice, performance depends on whether the model has learned the relevant visual-textual grounding, whether the prompt is complete and unambiguous, and whether the target concept is visually observable.

The gains conflate dataset scale/diversity with algorithmic novelty. Training VadCLIP on PreVAD narrows this issue somewhat, but the proposed architecture and losses appear incremental relative to existing CLIP-based weakly supervised VAD methods.

The dataset construction pipeline relies heavily on MLLMs/VLMs/LLMs, but the main paper provides limited evidence of annotation quality, error rates, inter-annotator agreement, prompt sensitivity, or failure modes. This is especially important because noisy descriptions directly affect the proposed paradigm.

Potential train-test contamination is a concern. PreVAD is collected from web/video-text sources, while many VAD benchmarks are also web-sourced; the paper does not clearly demonstrate deduplication against evaluation datasets at the video or near-duplicate clip level.

Baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying. Some results are taken from papers, some are reproduced, and training data differs substantially across methods; stronger controlled baselines with the same data, prompts, backbone, and training budget would better isolate the contribution.

The classification evaluation is limited to two datasets, while the paper claims broad open-world language-guided capability. It would be important to test richer natural-language definitions, paraphrases, exclusions, and conflicting definitions across all benchmarks.

Ethical and deployment issues are underdeveloped in the main manuscript, despite the surveillance setting, web-sourced videos, possible privacy/copyright concerns, and potential harms from user-defined anomaly detection.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time because the paper says data and code will be released but does not provide enough main-paper detail to independently verify dataset curation, prompts, exact training settings, and evaluation protocol.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem in video anomaly detection: anomaly definitions can change with user requirements, scene context, or policy, and existing fixed-label VAD setups do not handle this well.
The language-guided formulation is intuitive and potentially useful, since natural language is a practical interface for specifying anomaly definitions at inference time.
The authors assemble a large PreVAD dataset and evaluate zero-shot detection across seven existing datasets, which is broader than typical VAD evaluation.
The empirical tables show consistent gains over several reproduced and reported baselines, especially when comparing LaGoVAD trained on PreVAD against VadCLIP trained on the same dataset.
The paper includes ablations for the dataset, language guidance, dynamic video synthesis, and contrastive negative mining, which helps identify some contribution from each component.
weaknesses: The central open-world/concept-drift claim is not convincingly evaluated. Most experiments are standard cross-dataset zero-shot VAD using class-name prompts, while actual user-driven redefinition of anomalies is demonstrated mainly through a small qualitative example. This is insufficient evidence for the main claimed paradigm shift.

Novelty is limited. The method largely combines CLIP features, text-conditioned fusion, MIL losses, contrastive alignment, hard negative mining, and video mixing/synthesis, all of which are familiar ingredients. The paper does not clearly establish a technically substantial advance beyond adapting these components to VAD.

The dataset contribution is potentially valuable but under-validated. PreVAD relies heavily on foundation-model-generated descriptions and filtering, yet the manuscript gives little quantitative evidence of annotation accuracy, false-positive/false-negative rates, inter-annotator agreement, or human audit quality.

The evaluation may be confounded by dataset scale and diversity. The strongest improvements may come mostly from training on a much larger dataset rather than the proposed paradigm or architecture, and the paper does not fully disentangle these factors across all baselines.

The zero-shot benchmark has possible leakage and comparability concerns. PreVAD is collected from web/video-text sources, while several evaluation datasets are also web-sourced; the paper does not convincingly rule out overlap, near-duplicates, or shared source bias.

Baselines are incomplete for the main claim. The paper compares against VAD methods and some CLIP/action recognition baselines, but lacks stronger language-conditioned alternatives, prompt-tuned CLIP/RAG-style variants, LLM/VLM prompting baselines, and simple retrieval or similarity baselines under matched PreVAD training.

The ablation table is too compressed and does not sufficiently analyze sensitivity to prompts, anomaly-definition granularity, number of categories, conflicting definitions, ambiguous descriptions, or normal-class wording, all of which are crucial for language-guided open-world use.

The theoretical framing around avoiding concept drift is overstated. Conditioning on a text variable z does not by itself avoid concept drift unless the system can reliably interpret arbitrary user definitions and map them to visual evidence; the paper assumes much of this capability rather than proving it.

Reproducibility is limited in the main manuscript. Important details are deferred to the supplement, including prompts, implementation details, data curation details, and baseline reproduction settings; the paper also only says code and data will be released.

The paper overclaims practical open-world applicability. There is little discussion of safety, surveillance ethics, privacy, dataset bias, misuse risk, or failure modes, despite the application domain being sensitive.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored limitation of existing video anomaly detection: anomaly definitions can change across users, scenes, and policies, so fixed-label open-set/open-vocabulary formulations are insufficient.
The proposed language-guided formulation is conceptually appealing and practically useful, allowing anomaly definitions to be supplied at inference time via natural language.

PreVAD is a substantial dataset contribution: 35,279 videos with multi-level anomaly categories and anomaly descriptions, collected independently from common VAD benchmarks, which could be valuable for the community if released with sufficient metadata and quality controls.
The empirical evaluation is broad for VAD, covering seven zero-shot target datasets and both detection and classification metrics, with generally strong gains over reproduced CLIP/VAD baselines.

The method is reasonably simple and well motivated, combining CLIP features, language-video fusion, dynamic video synthesis, and contrastive hard negative mining; ablations suggest each component contributes to performance.
weaknesses: The central open-world/concept-drift claim is only partially evaluated. Most quantitative experiments use dataset-level class-name prompts on existing benchmarks, while true user-driven redefinition of the same visual pattern is supported mainly by two qualitative examples.

A large portion of the gains may come from PreVAD scale/diversity rather than the proposed paradigm or architecture. The paper includes some controls, but stronger comparisons under matched data, model capacity, and training budget would be needed to isolate the contribution.

Dataset construction relies heavily on foundation-model filtering and annotation, but the manuscript provides limited evidence of annotation accuracy, bias, duplicate removal, source overlap checks, or human audit statistics in the main paper.

Potential data contamination is a concern because videos are sourced from web/video-text datasets and streaming platforms while evaluation also uses public web-derived VAD datasets; stronger near-duplicate and semantic-overlap analysis is needed.

The formulation claims to avoid concept drift by conditioning on anomaly definitions, but this is stronger than what is demonstrated: performance can still fail under ambiguous prompts, unseen definitions, missing visual evidence, or shifts in normal context.

Baseline coverage is somewhat limited for the paper's claims. Some comparisons are reproduced, some are imported from papers, and more recent/general-purpose video-language or LLM-based detectors under identical prompting and data conditions would strengthen the evidence.
Classification results are mixed in places, e.g. UCF F1 does not clearly improve over the strongest same-data VadCLIP baseline, which weakens the claim of comprehensive improvement.

Reproducibility depends critically on the promised release of PreVAD, prompts, curation pipeline, and training details; without the supplementary material and released resources, several important implementation and data-quality details are hard to verify.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored problem in video anomaly detection: anomaly definitions can change with user intent, scene, or policy, so fixed-label/open-set formulations are insufficient.

The proposed language-guided formulation is clear and practically motivated, and the LaGoVAD model is a reasonable instantiation using text-conditioned detection, dynamic video synthesis, and contrastive negative mining.

PreVAD appears to be a substantial dataset contribution, with 35k videos, multi-level anomaly categories, and anomaly descriptions. If released as promised, it could be useful for weakly supervised and open-world VAD research.

The evaluation is broader than typical VAD papers, covering seven datasets in zero-shot settings, plus a dedicated drift@5 protocol. Including VadCLIP trained on PreVAD helps separate dataset effects from architectural effects.

Empirical results are consistently positive: LaGoVAD improves over reproduced and published baselines on most reported detection and classification metrics, and the ablations support the contributions of language guidance, dynamic synthesis, and negative mining.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat overstated. Conditioning anomaly detection on text definitions is closely related to open-vocabulary VAD, promptable VLM/LLM-based VAD, and language-guided retrieval/localization; the formal treatment of concept drift is mostly a reframing rather than a deep technical advance.

The concept-drift evaluation is artificial: Protocol 2 redefines subsets of existing anomaly categories as normal within the same dataset. This does not fully capture real deployment drift, where background context, operational policy, and subtle event semantics matter. The paper would benefit from human-written task definitions and cases where the same visual event is normal in one context and abnormal in another.

Dataset quality and reproducibility are not sufficiently established. Many labels/descriptions are generated by MLLMs/LLMs after filtering, but the paper reports limited quantitative annotation quality, inter-annotator agreement, error analysis, or auditing of generated descriptions.

There are nontrivial ethical and legal concerns around public web/surveillance videos, violent content, people in videos, and copyright/licensing. The statement that public sources imply no privacy or ethical issues is inadequate for a top-tier venue.

Some comparisons remain imperfect. LaGoVAD benefits from a large new pretraining dataset with text annotations, while several baselines are not naturally designed for user-defined anomaly descriptions. The paper includes a VadCLIP-on-PreVAD control, but stronger adaptation/fine-tuning of promptable baselines would make the evidence more convincing.
Several reported classification results remain weak, especially UCF F1, suggesting that semantic category recognition under the proposed paradigm is still limited despite strong detection numbers.

The method itself is technically incremental: CLIP features, transformer temporal/fusion modules, MIL losses, video concatenation augmentation, and contrastive learning are familiar components. The main strength is the system/dataset/evaluation package rather than a novel algorithmic idea.

Release details are vague. The paper says dataset and code will be released, but the dataset statement later mentions releasing annotations and download scripts; it is unclear whether videos, exact splits, prompts, generated descriptions, and retrieval/cleaning metadata will be fully reproducible.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant limitation of standard VAD settings: anomaly definitions can change with user intent, deployment context, or policy, and language conditioning is a natural interface for this problem.

The proposed PreVAD dataset is large relative to existing VAD datasets and appears to cover a broader range of domains and anomaly types, which could be useful if released with sufficient documentation and licensing clarity.

The paper includes several cross-dataset zero-shot evaluations and ablations, and the attempt to separate general open-world evaluation from a concept-drift-oriented protocol is directionally valuable.
weaknesses: The central conceptual contribution is overstated. Modeling predictions as conditioned on both video and a textual definition is a fairly direct extension of vision-language conditioning, and the paper does not provide a sufficiently rigorous formulation or analysis showing that this actually resolves concept drift rather than merely adding prompts as another input.

The evaluation strongly confounds dataset scale with method quality. Much of the gain appears attributable to training on PreVAD, and the method-level improvements over strong baselines trained on PreVAD are modest in several places. The paper needs better controlled comparisons, including stronger architectures trained on the same data and prompt-conditioned variants of existing methods.

The proposed concept-drift protocol is not fully convincing. Randomly treating unselected anomaly categories as normal is an artificial relabeling setup and may create label noise rather than realistic drift. It also tests category filtering more than open-ended user-defined anomaly semantics.

Baseline comparisons are uneven and sometimes unfair. Several compared methods were not designed to accept dynamic language definitions, while LLM/VLM baselines are converted to frame scores in ad hoc ways. The paper does not show that each baseline is adapted, prompted, and tuned as strongly as the proposed method.

Dataset quality and leakage risks are insufficiently addressed. PreVAD is built partly from existing video-text datasets and web sources, but the paper provides limited evidence about duplicate removal, overlap with evaluation datasets, copyright/licensing, privacy, or distributional contamination. These issues are especially important for a dataset-centered contribution.

Annotation quality is under-supported. Many descriptions are generated by MLLMs with category-constrained prompts, but there are no strong human validation statistics, inter-annotator agreement, caption accuracy estimates, or systematic analysis of hallucination and category ambiguity.

The paper’s claims about state-of-the-art open-world performance are stronger than the evidence. Results mix AUC and AP across datasets, lack confidence intervals or significance testing, and rely on manual prompts whose robustness is only lightly explored.

Some reported classification results raise concerns: for example, UCF multi-class F1 remains very low despite improved accuracy, suggesting class imbalance or poor fine-grained recognition that is not adequately discussed.

The dynamic video synthesis module may introduce unrealistic concatenated videos and pseudo-labels, and the paper does not sufficiently analyze whether the resulting temporal artifacts help genuine anomaly localization or simply regularize benchmark-specific biases.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time. The paper says code and data will be released, but the current manuscript lacks enough detail on data filtering thresholds, prompt sets, exact category definitions, train/eval splits, and baseline reproduction choices to independently verify the main claims.

Ethical and legal considerations are underdeveloped for a large web-collected surveillance/anomaly dataset containing violence, accidents, and potentially identifiable people. The paper needs a much more serious discussion of consent, privacy, harmful use, licensing, and dataset governance.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely limitation of video anomaly detection: anomaly definitions can change by deployment context or user intent. Framing this as language-guided open-world VAD under concept drift is compelling and practically motivated.

The proposed PreVAD dataset is a substantial contribution in scale and diversity, with 35k videos, multi-level taxonomy, and anomaly descriptions. This could be useful beyond the specific model if released with clear documentation.
The empirical evaluation is broad, covering seven external datasets in a zero-shot setting, plus a separate concept-drift protocol. This is much stronger than typical single-dataset VAD evaluations.

LaGoVAD is technically plausible and well aligned with the task formulation: conditioning detection on text definitions, dynamic video synthesis to address anomaly-duration bias, and contrastive negative mining for multimodal alignment are reasonable design choices.
Ablations indicate that both the dataset and the proposed modules contribute to performance, and comparisons include several relevant VAD, open-vocabulary, and MLLM-based baselines.
weaknesses: The central concept-drift evaluation is still somewhat artificial: redefining subsets of category labels as normal/abnormal does not fully test fine-grained user-defined anomaly concepts where the same visual event changes label depending on context, policy, or scene. Prompt compliance is not systematically evaluated.

The method contribution is less novel than the problem formulation and dataset. Architecturally, LaGoVAD is largely a CLIP/Transformer multimodal VAD model with regularization losses; the strongest contribution appears to be data and task setup rather than a fundamentally new modeling technique.

Dataset quality and reproducibility need stronger evidence. Many annotations and descriptions are generated by MLLMs/LLMs, but the paper provides limited quantitative validation of description correctness, inter-annotator agreement, label noise, or failure modes of the human-AI pipeline.

The paper makes overly broad ethical and privacy claims. Public web videos, surveillance streams, traffic cameras, violent incidents, and accident footage can involve privacy, consent, copyright, and harm concerns; stating that there are no privacy or ethical issues is not sufficiently supported.

Potential data leakage or near-duplicate overlap with benchmark test sets is not adequately audited, especially because PreVAD is collected from broad public web/video-text sources and existing media collections.

Some reported metrics are uneven. For example, UCF multi-class F1 remains very low and is not clearly improved over the strongest PreVAD-trained baseline, suggesting limited classification reliability despite strong detection results.

The evaluation of some datasets is potentially nonstandard or hard to interpret, such as normalizing predictions on DoTA because it contains only abnormal videos. This weakens comparability of the aggregate claims.

Baseline fairness is not fully established. Several results are reproduced with different feature choices, training sets, prompts, and post-processing assumptions; stronger details and sensitivity analyses would improve confidence.
The paper would benefit from deeper analysis of failure cases, robustness to prompt wording, out-of-taxonomy natural-language definitions, and ambiguity in user-specified anomaly descriptions.
